children: 0500 GMT - Fitch Ratings expects the oil market to return to a substantial surplus in 2027. While it expects oil prices to fall next year, Fitch has raised its 2027 forecast for oil to US$70 a barrel from $65 a barrel to reflect the longer-than-anticipated Middle East conflict and the implications for the geopolitical risk premium. Analysts Brian Coulton and Alex Muscatelli acknowledge a high level of uncertainty around these projections. Assuming a deal between the U.S. and Iran takes shape in 1Q of 2027, supply and demand fundamentals could play a bigger role in determining oil prices. On the upside, geopolitical uncertainties could result in oil prices averaging $85 a barrel next year, while on the downside, a rapid recovery in supply could see prices fall to $55 a barrel, they say in a report. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0442 GMT - Fitch Ratings raises its forecast for U.S. government bond yields by 30bp to 4.8% by end-2026 and expects yields to remain at this level through the end of 2027. "We expect yields to edge down a bit from the 5% rate seen in recent weeks as oil prices fall back, but they will remain well above the levels seen before the U.S.-Iran war," say analysts Brian Coulton and Alex Muscatelli in a report. The Fed delivered its first rate rise in over three years in September and Fitch anticipates a further 25bp increase in December, taking rates to 4.25%. "We expect the Fed to hold rates in 2027, which would leave rates at the end of next year a full 125bp higher than we were forecasting in June," they add. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0421 GMT - Fitch Ratings says it has lowered its 2026 growth forecast for China by 0.1pp to 4.5%, citing falling fixed-asset investment and weak consumer spending dampening domestic demand. Domestic indicators have weakened in recent months, with fixed-asset investment falling and the housing slump deepening, say analysts Brian Coulton and Alex Muscatelli in a report. Retail sales and credit growth have also slowed as the household sector faces deleveraging pressures. Fiscal support to growth has been modest. However, China's export performance remains stellar, cushioning the slowdown, they add. (monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0416 GMT - Some Asia-Pacific central banks may tighten policy further this year to contain inflation and support foreign-exchange rates, S&P Global Ratings economists say in a note. Higher oil prices are likely to lift inflation modestly, while food prices could rise further due to El Nino. Meanwhile, regional currencies weakened significantly in 1H, though the depreciation pressure has abated over 3Q, they note. Still, the majority of these currencies remain weaker against the U.S. dollar than at the start of the year. In the economists' baseline outlook, they expect monetary tightening to be modest where inflation and exchange-rate pressures aren't severe. S&P expects central banks in Australia, India, South Korea, Taiwan and the Philippines to raise their rates by 25 basis points each in the remainder of 2026. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0331 GMT - Emerging-market debt is no longer the narrow distressed-debt niche of the 1990s, but a powerful engine of global growth, offering diverse opportunities, Eastspring Investments says in a note. The percentage of investment grade-rated dollar-denominated emerging-market sovereign bonds rose to above 50% in 2025 up from 0% in 1991, the asset manager says. Meanwhile, in several developed markets, larger fiscal needs and structurally higher social spending may challenge the path back to sustainably lower inflation, it says. Artificial-intelligence disruption, geopolitical tensions, shifting trade alliances and energy security concerns are creating greater dispersion across growth, inflation and policy rates within the emerging markets, Eastspring says. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0258 GMT - The Singapore dollar weakens against its U.S. counterpart ahead of the city-state's August CPI data release. The inflation reading will be the final key data point before the Monetary Authority of Singapore's policy meeting in October. Markets expect core inflation to edge higher to 2.2% on year in August from 2.0% in July, UOB's Lee Sue Ann and Quek Ser Leang say in a note. Signs of inflationary pressures broadening beyond energy-related components and rising food prices could reinforce expectations of further MAS tightening, they add. The U.S. dollar is 0.1% higher at 1.2756 Singapore dollars, LSEG data show.(amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0204 GMT - There is a strong floor under gold prices around $3,800/oz, according to BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions. While the precious metal faces pressure from U.S. dollar strength and "a hawkish turn in U.S. Fed policy," geopolitical risks remain high and central bank purchases of gold continue, it says. BMI reiterates a 2026 average gold-price forecast of $4,400/oz. The price has averaged $4,555/oz year to date, it says. Spot gold is down 0.4% at $4,340.65/oz. (rhiannon.hoyle@wsj.com; @RhiannonHoyle)

0141 GMT - The U.S.-China leadership summit is likely to focus on tech and trade, paving the way for lower tariffs on nonsensitive goods, Aberdeen Investments' Robert Gilhooly says in a note. Preparatory meetings between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng suggest that some progress has already been made on trade, the senior emerging markets economist says. That could pave the way for lower tariffs on some nonsensitive goods, while China may offer to buy more U.S. farm products, energy products and Boeing aircraft, he says. An artificial-intelligence-safety dialogue or memorandum is plausible, but it would probably be short on details, Gilhooly says. (kosaku.narioka@wsj.com; @kosakunarioka)

0133 GMT - Asian currencies consolidate against the dollar. Crude oil prices are weakening amid a de-escalation of Middle East tensions and optimism that oil supplies from Saudi Arabia through the Red Sea could be restored within days, says Samer Hasn of XS.com in a note. Declining oil prices typically benefit these currencies as many countries in Asia are net oil importers. The dollar is 0.1% higher at 157.58 yen but 0.25% lower at 1,350.60 won, while the Australian dollar is flat at US$0.7110, LSEG data show. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0042 GMT - South Korea's downstream oil and gas sector is likely to remain stable in 2026, despite pressure from elevated freight costs and geopolitical risks, BMI says in a report. The Fitch Solutions unit sees the country shifting toward a broader energy-security strategy focused on reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern crude. The government aims to reduce the Middle Eastern share of crude imports to 60% or less, from 69.1% in 2024, it notes. Latest energy import data show the country's increased sourcing flexibility, with the Middle East accounting for 62.8% of crude imports in the January-May period and the Americas, including the U.S., accounting for 26.6% in May, it adds. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com)

0037 GMT - Bitcoin rises in early Asia trade, staying around 8-month highs above $86,000. A sustained break above that line would signal a more solid recovery after several false starts. Bitcoin's gains this month stand at around 10%--far below August's rally but still notable as they have come despite a recent Fed rate increase. The cryptocurrency has recovered more than 14% since the hike, showing greater resilience in a restrictive monetary environment, says Antonio Di Giacomo at XS.com. Support is coming from easing oil prices that have partially tamed inflation concerns, moderating Treasury yields and institutional capital inflows, he says. Still, risks remain, with the $87,500 area representing the first major resistance, followed by the $90,000 psychological barrier. Bitcoin rises 0.3% to $86,482. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

2003 GMT - Bond markets trade sideways but the U.S. Treasury borrowing costs keep rising. A two-year notes auction has a yield of 4.787%, the highest paid by the Treasury since May 2024. Demand was robust, nonetheless. A five-year auction is scheduled for tomorrow, followed by a seven-year tender on Thursday. Oil prices fall around 1% amid hopes of a deal to normalize trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Inflation expectations as measured by one-year swaps decline to 2.3% from 2.6% two weeks ago, but remain above the Fed's 2% target, according to LSEG. The 10-year yield rises 0.004 percentage point to 4.966%, while the two-year slips 0.001 point to 4.749%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)
